entities.name: And Then There Were None
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
And Then There Were None (1939) is a mystery novel by English writer Agatha Christie — her own choice as the most difficult of her books to write. It was first published in the United Kingdom by Collins Crime Club in November 1939, initially under a different title, and is the best-selling mystery novel of all time with over 100 million copies sold.

Ten people are invited to a remote island off the Devon coast under various pretexts, only to find themselves cut off from the mainland. A gramophone recording accuses each guest of having caused someone's death without facing legal consequences. One by one, the guests are murdered according to the rhyme of a children's song, with no apparent killer among the survivors. Christie's genius lay in constructing a locked-room mystery with no surviving detective — the solution revealed only through a postscript written by the murderer.

The novel's enduring power rests on its structural elegance — a closed-universe problem in pure logic — and its unsettling moral philosophy: the characters are guilty people who escaped justice, raising questions about vigilante punishment, the reliability of guilt, and the horror of isolation. It has been adapted for film, television, radio, and stage over twenty times. Christie's ability to sustain suspense while systematically eliminating all possible suspects made it one of the most influential works in the history of crime fiction, defining the 'whodunit' form that dominated 20th-century popular literature.
